Written design doc at docs/secret-custody-design.md. Three options evaluated: (A) Native-held key — no hw-backed key accessible to shell UID, all stable sources (ro.*) readable by attacker, prior NDK secrets lib removed for app_process stability; (B) App-decrypts-over-IPC — no improvement against shell-UID attacker, re-exposes plaintext on loopback; (C) Property-derived key — marginal protection against file-copy only, OTA risk; (D) Accept current model [CHOSEN]. Decision: mode-600 shell-owned single file + Track0 IPC lockdown is the correct primary defense. Full at-rest encryption requires HSM not available on BYD DiLink v3 for shell-UID processes. Option C deferred as future work if file-copy threat materializes.

### The coverage problem this task found, and the fix

Building the 12 typed service clients against `FakeRpcClient` (per "use the shared fake, do not write your own") initially left every wrapper method's own response-decoding closure — `(json) => SomeResponse()..mergeFromProto3Json(json)` — unexercised, because `stub()` hands back the pre-stubbed value directly and never calls the `decode` argument at all. Coverage of `lib/rpc/services/*.dart` sat at roughly 50% and the overall Dart figure was ~66%, which would have violated this task's own "not lower than the previous task's figure" (92.31%) requirement. Fixed by adding `stubJson()` to `FakeRpcClient` (BladeWatch-ncbb.5's fake, extended here): it stores a raw proto3Json value and actually runs it through the caller's `decode` callback, exercising the real logic instead of bypassing it — a genuinely useful addition for any future test that wants to prove a controller handles a specific (or malformed/partial) response shape, not just a coverage workaround. Added tests for `stubJson` itself (decode runs, `null` passes through cleanly for an empty response body, throws `StateError` if `call()` is invoked with no decode function, and that it correctly supersedes/is superseded by `stub()`/`stubError()`/`stubTimeout()` on the same key).

inspected the generated `lookupAppLocalizations()` — `Locale('zh','CN')` still resolves to

extending the synthesized `AppLocalizationsZh` base only for any key the subclass doesn't
override), same for `pt`/`BR` and `zh`/`TW`. The synthesized fallback is only reached for a
language-only match with no country code.

  confirmation) — Android's ClipboardManager is synchronous; Flutter's Clipboard API is
  Future-based only because of the platform-channel round trip, and (found empirically) that
  Future never resolves inside `flutter_test`'s environment regardless of `pump()`/
  `pumpAndSettle()` count, since nothing schedules a frame while it's pending. Not awaiting is
  both correct UX (instant confirmation, matching native's perceived synchronicity) and
  resolved the test hang.

## Fix applied

Went with option 1 from the bug report (the preferred, simpler fix): mirror deviceId and
tokenEpoch into the secret store's "auth" section, alongside deviceSecret, so
secret_get_section (the only IPC command JwtMinter.kt can reach) returns everything it needs
in one call — no protocol change, JwtMinter.kt is untouched.

- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/auth/AuthManager.java — writeToConfig() now
  calls a new package-private writeSecretStoreMirror(state), which writes deviceSecret
  (exclusively, as before) AND deviceId/tokenEpoch (new) into SecretConfigBridge's "auth"
  section, using the same KEY_DEVICE_ID/KEY_TOKEN_EPOCH constants AuthState already defines.
  Confirmed via TcpCommandServer.java's secret_get_section handler (line ~461) that it returns
  store().loadSection(section) raw and unfiltered, so these two fields flow straight through to
  the IPC response once written — no changes needed there. On failure partway through (mirror
  write fails after the secret write succeeded, or the follow-on UnifiedConfigManager write
  fails), rollbackSecretWrite() undoes the secret-store side so a partial write is never left
  behind.
- app/src/main/java/com/loabletech/bladewatch/config/SecretConfigBridge.kt — added a
  `directStoreForTest` test seam (mirrors SecretConfigStore's own existing
  `legacyPathForTest` seam) to getString/putString/putLong/delete — the 4 methods
  AuthManager's auth read/write path actually calls. Needed because canWriteDirectly()/
  canReadDirectly() hard-require shell UID 2000 (meaningless off a real device) and the IPC
  fallback would otherwise block a JVM test for up to 30s per call
  (DaemonReadinessChecker.waitUntilReady(30_000) polls a real TCP port that's never open on a
  dev machine). Scoped to only the 4 methods actually needed — getLong/getBoolean/putBoolean/
  loadSection are untouched since nothing on this path calls them.

## Why writeToConfig() itself wasn't the direct test target

writeToConfig() also calls UnifiedConfigManager.updateSection(), a separate class with its own
config path hardcoded to a real device path
(/storage/emulated/0/BladeWatch/data/bladewatch_config.json) and no test seam of its own.
Exercising it from a JVM test on this dev machine would have tried real File.mkdirs()/write
calls against that absolute path — unrelated to this bug, already untested before this task
(no UnifiedConfigManagerTest file exists), and a real (if probably-harmless, given normal Unix
permissions) risk of touching the host filesystem. Rather than add a second test seam to an
unrelated class just to route around it, the new secret-store-mirroring logic was factored into
its own package-private method (writeSecretStoreMirror) that touches only SecretConfigBridge,
and is tested directly and completely in isolation. writeToConfig()'s own UnifiedConfigManager
half is unchanged from before this task and remains covered by existing behavior only, same as
prior to this fix.

## The user's explicit decision (AskUserQuestion, not autonomous)

The ADB Console needs to talk raw ADB protocol to adbd on 127.0.0.1:5555 — there is no `shell`
IPC command (removed as an RCE fix, TcpCommandServer.java's uy93.2 comment) and this class of
shell-execution capability was deliberately walked back elsewhere in this codebase. Presented 3
options (pub.dev ADB package / defer the whole screen / hand-roll a minimal Dart client); the
user chose to hand-roll it. Delivered as scoped: the wire protocol (framing, connect/auth/
shell state machine, socket I/O) is 100% hand-rolled Dart with zero third-party ADB packages;
the ONE piece not hand-rolled is the ADB/mincrypt public-key struct format (Montgomery-
precomputed, not meaningfully "protocol logic"), reused from dadb (a library already vetted and
shipped in the main app) rather than risk an unverifiable-without-a-device bug in a from-scratch
reimplementation of that specific format.

## Architecture: push-to-poll translation

Native drives everything off `LocationListener` callbacks the OS fires, plus a separately-scheduled stale-check `Handler`. `LocationController` is polled instead: `LocationScreen` owns a `Timer.periodic(1s)` (matching native's own `requestLocationUpdates(provider, 1_000L, ...)` minTime) calling `poll()`, which folds sample-arrival, provider-enabled/disabled edge detection, and the periodic staleness sweep into one tick. `LocationServiceChannel` (Kotlin) stays a thin OS-primitive wrapper — deliberately not reimplementing the state machine natively — so the actual behavior lives in Dart, fully covered and fake-clock-testable. Provider precedence (prefer GPS, fall back to NETWORK) was likewise moved from native's `selectedProvider()` into Dart for the same reason: `LocationServiceChannel`, like `NetworkInfoChannel` before it, is Android-framework-bound and excluded from the Kotlin coverage gate, so keeping the precedence *decision* in Kotlin would leave it untested.

`effectiveState` vs. `state` mirrors a real native distinction: `LocationTileFailure` (shown when offline while otherwise Fresh/Stale) is never stored back into native's `currentState` — `LocationMapController.render()` computes it fresh every call, purely for display. Reproduced as two separate controller members: `state` (raw GPS state machine) and `effectiveState` (the same, downgraded on read when offline) — the screen renders `effectiveState`.

`LocationUiStateMapper`/`LocationPanelModel` were not ported as a class — native's version returns literal English strings, which this port's ARB-only rule forbids in a pure-Dart model. The same state→presentation decision logic lives in a private `_bannerFor()` switch at the screen layer instead, each arm resolving an ARB key. `LocationError`'s subtitle is the one exception: shown verbatim (no ARB wrapping), matching `TripsController`'s `SyncOutcome.error` precedent — raw diagnostic text, not composed prose.

Excluding `LocationServiceChannel` by exact class name left its anonymous `LocationListener` object — compiled as the synthetic nested class `LocationServiceChannel$listener$1` — still counted against the gate (`koverVerify` failed at 99%, not 100%). ## Defensive error handling added beyond the native 1:1 port

Native's `LocationGpsController` never has to handle "the channel itself is unavailable" — it calls `LocationManager` in-process. This Dart port's channel calls can throw (`PlatformChannelError`) when no native handler is registered (exactly the situation `widget_test.dart`'s daemon-less smoke test exercises). `start()` catches and surfaces `LocationError`; `poll()` catches and silently skips that tick (the next one, one second away, retries) rather than flipping the whole screen to an error state over a single transient hiccup — same defensive posture `DiagnosticsController`'s per-tile try/catch already establishes elsewhere in this port.

## The central architectural finding: native reads the filesystem directly, this port can't, so it follows the web reference instead

`RecordingsFragment`/`RecordingLibraryFragment` call `RecordingScanner`/`java.io.File` directly — zero RPC calls in either fragment (a genuine surprise, since the task description's own hint suggested checking which of `RecordingsService`'s 8 RPCs are used). Native has this option because the app process is co-located with the daemon and both can read `/storage/emulated/0/BladeWatch/...` directly; this Flutter APK cannot. Rather than invent a new IPC surface, this port mirrors `web/src/app/pages/recording/recording.component.ts` — the **already-shipped, sanctioned** Angular translation of this exact screen: fetch the whole catalog once (`ListRecordings({type: '', pageSize: 1000})`), filter segment/date/chips entirely client-side. `RecordingsApiHandler.java` clamps `pageSize` to 50 server-side regardless of what's requested — a real, already-accepted limit neither reference client (native's own unlimited scan aside) works around, and neither does this one.

Header aggregate counts (today/total/dashcam/surveillance counts, total bytes) come from `GetStats` (server-computed over the *full* catalog), not the `ListRecordings` page (capped at 50 — using it for totals would silently undercount). The "today" count has no `RecordingStats` field, so it's computed client-side from the same `ListRecordings` payload already fetched for the grid, same 50-item caveat.

## Two real bugs found and fixed via widget tests

1. **The controller's injectable fake clock wasn't actually reaching the widgets.** `RecordingsController.nowMs` existed for deterministic today/yesterday tests, but `_DateRow`/`_RecordingsGrid` called `DateTime.now()` directly — harmless in production (real clock either way) but it silently broke fake-clock testability exactly where it mattered. A widget test asserting "Yesterday" renders after `goYesterday()` caught it; fixed by exposing `RecordingsController.nowMs` publicly and reading it from both widgets.
2. **A real hit-test bug in the player, present on a real device too.** `GestureDetector(child: Center(child: AspectRatio(...)))`'s default `deferToChild` behavior only registers taps inside the letterboxed video rectangle itself — tapping the surrounding black bars (most of a 16:9 clip in a taller window) would silently do nothing. Fixed with `behavior: HitTestBehavior.opaque`.

## A new test infrastructure piece: a hand-rolled fake `VideoPlayerPlatform`

`video_player` ships no fake of its own for widget tests (the standard federated-plugin testing gap). `test/fakes/fake_video_player_platform.dart` is a minimal one: enough for `VideoPlayerController.initialize()` to resolve and play/pause/seek to update in-memory state, no real decoder. ## Architecture decision (documented in full in docs/build-and-operations.md)

Dart owns the WebSocket connection and the 3 `StreamService` RPCs the screen actually calls (Enable/SetViewMode/GetQuality — of 7 total; Disable/GetStatus/SetQuality/GetViewMode have no call site in this screen either, native or here). Kotlin owns only `MediaCodec` decode into a Flutter `Texture`. This diverges from the task's "port LiveStreamClient wholesale, just swap the Surface" framing for two reasons, not one preference:

1. **Unavoidable regardless of preference**: `LiveStreamClient.kt`'s RPC calls and JWT minting go through the main app's `ConnectClientProvider`/`AuthManager` singletons, which the separate Flutter APK (net.bladewatch.flutter vs net.bladewatch.app — different classloaders, shared UID only) cannot reach at all.
2. **A genuine choice**: the WebSocket handshake/frame-reassembly itself *could* have been ported to new native networking code instead of using `dart:io`'s `WebSocket`. It was not, because `dart:io`'s WebSocket is RFC 6455 compliant and already proven against this exact server (the Angular SPA's own standard browser WebSocket client). This keeps the new native surface to exactly the one thing Dart cannot do (hardware H.264 decode) — the smallest surface for the task's own "a leaked MediaCodec is unrecoverable" warning to apply to.

Corrections made along the way, all verified against source rather than assumed:
- `stream.proto`'s own comment claims port 8887; `CameraDaemon.HTTP_PORT = 8080` is the real port (same port as HTTP/ConnectRPC). The client connects to `ws://127.0.0.1:8080/ws`.
- Only 5 directions exist (Mosaic/Front/Right/Rear/Left) — `stream.proto`'s `ViewMode` has a 6th value (`VIEW_MODE_RAW`), but `LiveViewModels.kt`'s own `LiveViewDirection` enum never exposes it. Not added here either.
